growth_story.headline: Political crises have cut short every growth spurt, and Madagascar's income per person is still 45.9 percent below its 1971 peak.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in Madagascar peaked in 1971 and, 54 years on, is still 45.9 percent below that level; it is lower today than in 1960, the first year of the record. From 1990 to 2002 it fell by 2.0 percent a year on average, an era opened and closed by political crises: income per person dropped 9.1 percent in 1991 and 15.0 percent in 2002. Since 2003 growth has averaged 0.6 percent a year: a rebound of 6.6 percent in 2003 and steady gains through 2008 ended with a fall of 6.8 percent in 2009, when a long political crisis began and aid and trade preferences were suspended. Income per person then barely moved for years, fell 9.5 percent in 2020 as the pandemic hit, and has recovered slowly since, averaging 0.3 percent a year over 2016-2025. World Bank studies describe a repeating pattern in which political crises reverse the gains of each growth spell, while the population grows faster than output.

threads.title: Crises that end each boom
threads.text: World Bank studies find that political crises in 1972, 1991, 2001-02 and 2009-13 each interrupted a period of growth. Income per person fell in each of those crisis years, including 9.1 percent in 1991, 15.0 percent in 2002 and 6.8 percent in 2009.

threads.title: The long 2009-13 crisis
threads.text: The crisis that began in 2009 lasted for years, and aid and trade preferences were suspended. Income per person fell 6.8 percent in 2009, kept falling in 2010 and 2011, and has still not regained its 2008 level.

threads.title: Low productivity, unreliable power
threads.text: The World Bank reports that productivity has long been falling and is now among the lowest in the world. Firms name unreliable electricity and water, weak access to finance and political uncertainty as obstacles, and the IMF still described outages and water shortages in 2026.

threads.text: Madagascar is again in a political transition, under a new administration that has redirected investment projects. It came as cyclones struck early in 2026 and the war in the Middle East pushed up oil prices.

since_last_year.text: Growth in income per person slowed to 0.6 percent in 2025, from 1.8 in 2024. In September 2025 the IMF pointed to outside shocks and problems in the mining sector. By September 2026 it added cyclones early in the year, higher oil prices from the war in the Middle East, and a political transition.

growth_story.tension: The IMF reports that output kept growing in 2025 and expects faster growth in 2026, helped by rebuilding after the cyclones. Income per person tells a flatter story: it rose 1.8 percent in 2024 and 0.6 percent in 2025, and averaged 0.3 percent a year over 2016-2025, because population growth absorbs most of the gain. World Bank studies note that since independence the population has grown much faster than output.
